chunks: "I'd describe the classic graphics pipeline as a stream of data going through stages. The application and driver send vertices and draw commands.
First the vertex shader runs on every vertex: it transforms positions from model space through the camera and projection into clip space.
Then primitive assembly groups vertices into triangles, clips them against the view volume, culls back-facing ones, and maps to screen coordinates.
The rasterizer is next, a fixed-function stage that works out which pixels each triangle covers and interpolates attributes like color and texture coordinates across it.
Each covered pixel becomes a fragment, and the fragment shader runs on it: that's where lighting and texture sampling happen.
Finally the raster output stage does the depth test, stencil and blending, and writes the result into the framebuffer in memory, which the display controller scans out.
Vertex and fragment stages are programmable and run on the same shader cores. Rasterizer, texture units and ROPs are fixed-function.
Mobile GPUs usually use tile-based rendering, which splits the screen into small tiles and does depth and blending on chip, so each pixel is written to DRAM once.
Compute shaders bypass most of this and just use the shader cores."
